title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 9: BATTLES OF THE DAMNED
keywords: the furtive finger that triggered his arrest
manifestly and grossly disadvantageous to the government
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- three cases in which CJP fought, mostly in dissent, for the rights of the accused and against what he saw as escape hatches for the powerful: warrantless arrests and searches, the defense of obedience to a superior's order, and the acquittal of Imelda R. Marcos of graft

The warrantless-arrest battles: his concurrence with Justice Davide's unanimous acquittal in Malacat v. Court of Appeals and his dissent, joined by Justices Melo and Puno, in People v. Montilla, where he argued that a tip from an informer is not personal knowledge and cannot substitute for a warrant

His dissent in Tabuena and Peralta v. Sandiganbayan, where an 8-6 majority acquitted the MIAA officials who remitted P55 million on President Marcos' memorandum: he called the defense of superior orders an 'internationally discredited Nazi defense' already debunked at Nuremberg by the test of whether moral choice was possible

His 27-page dissent from the en banc acquittal of Imelda R. Marcos in the LRTA-PGHFI lease-and-sublease cases, arguing that 'entering' into a contract is not the same as 'signing' it, that the two contracts are themselves the proof of gross and manifest disadvantage, and that the Sandiganbayan's procedural irregularities did not oust it of jurisdiction
sub_topics: The framing question of criminal procedure and constitutional law: the delicate line between a valid arrest and an unlawful one without a warrant, taken up en banc in Malacat and Montilla

Malacat: the Manila trial court convicted him of illegal possession of a hand grenade after a surveillance team arrested a man with 'shifty eyes' at Plaza Miranda who tried to flee; the Court through Justice Davide acquitted him because a lawful arrest must precede the search -- 'the process cannot be reversed'
The unanimous holding that there was neither in flagrante delicto nor hot pursuit, for want of personal knowledge or an overt physical act, so the search could not be incidental to a lawful arrest

Malacat's reliance on People v. Mengote, where 'darting eyes and his hand on his abdomen' were held insufficient, and the Court's warning that summarily arresting a man holding his abdomen 'simply cannot be done in a free society'

CJP's full Concurring Opinion in Malacat comparing it with four decisions he had authored -- Manalili, Encinada, Lacerna and Cuison -- and concluding that convicting a man on his queer behavior alone would be 'wrong, unjust and inhuman'

Montilla: a month and a half later, an appellant was seized at dawn alighting from a jeepney in Barangay Salitran, Dasmariñas, Cavite with 28 kilos of marijuana, on a tip from an unnamed informer; the majority through Justice Regalado upheld the arrest and urged 'a realistic appreciation of the physical and tactical problems' of law enforcers
CJP's refusal of that appeal despite his esteem for Justice Regalado: his duty as a jurist was 'to uphold the law, defend the rights and liberties of the people and be consistent in my rulings'

His first ground: under the in flagrante delicto rule the officer must have personal knowledge and the offense must occur in his presence -- there was no overt act, no bulkiness suggesting a firearm, no peculiar smell suggesting marijuana

His second ground: the hot pursuit rule requires that a crime actually have been committed, citing People v. Burgos, and the case closely parallels People v. Aminnudin, where 'the furtive finger' of the informer, not any outward indication, triggered the arrest

His third ground: raw intelligence information cannot justify a warrantless arrest; the police had the tip at 2:00 p.m. the previous day, and Administrative Circulars 13 and 19, s. 1987 allow warrant applications after office hours and on a Sunday

His attack on the majority's internal contradiction: if the information was too bare for a warrant, it was far too bare for a warrantless arrest, since the law requires stricter grounds for warrantless arrests than for the issuance of warrants

His warning that treating 'reliable tips' as probable cause is a dangerous precedent leaving everyone at the mercy of informants 'reminiscent of the makapilis during the Japanese occupation,' and would let officers manufacture urgency by delaying their tips
The saving fact that the Montilla pronouncement was only an obiter, both sides agreeing that the search issue was waived by the failure to raise it before arraignment

Tabuena and Peralta: by 8 to 6 with one justice not taking part, the Court acquitted the MIAA officials of malversation of P55 million paid to the Office of the President as alleged partial payment of MIAA's obligation to PNCC, treating obedience to a superior's lawful order as a justifying circumstance

CJP's dissent, joining Justices Davide, Romero and Puno: the Nuremberg Tribunal's judgment of October 1, 1946 and the 1947 UN General Assembly resolution both hold that superior orders do not excuse where 'a moral choice was in fact possible'

His comparison of circumstances: the Nuremberg defendants were military officers facing court martial and death in wartime, while Tabuena and Peralta were civilians after martial law had been lifted, who could have defied the order or resigned -- the cash delivery to the President's private secretary itself gave them a moral choice to refuse

His institutional warning that resurrecting the defense would deprive the Court of moral authority to convict any subaltern of the martial law dictator, and his sequencing of virtues: 'justice first before mercy,' with pardon lying elsewhere

Marcos v. Sandiganbayan: the 1984 LRTA leases of the Pasay and Carriedo lots to the PGHFI, chaired by Mrs. Marcos herself, and the immediate subleases to TNCC at seven times and to Joy Mart at twice the rental, producing five Informations under RA 3019

The procedural history: conviction in the Second and Fifth Informations in 1993, a 3-2 Division ruling in January 1998 acquitting Dans and affirming Marcos' conviction, referral of her Motion for Reconsideration to the banc after the Third Division was reduced to four members, and oral argument on September 10, 1998

The October 6, 1998 acquittal penned by Justice Purisima: the prosecution failed to prove the elements of Section 3(g) because Mrs. Marcos signed as PGHFI chair and not on behalf of the government, and because a rental disparity alone is 'purely speculative' without a standard -- 'Gross is a comparative term'

The second ground of acquittal: the 'procedural flaws' in the Sandiganbayan -- the creation and abrupt dissolution of the Special Division of five, and the discussion of the cases in a Quezon City restaurant without Justices Atienza and Amores and in the presence of a non-member

The concurrences of Justices Kapunan and Bellosillo on the insufficiency of evidence of fair and reasonable rentals, including Kapunan's account of Chief Prosecutor Tamayo's admission at oral argument, and Justice Vitug's vote to remand rather than acquit

CJP's answer to the 'signing' argument: the law says 'entering,' not 'signing,' and those who authorized, approved or assented are equally accountable -- she contracted 'virtually with herself' as chair of both lessor and lessee, and never sought rescission once the disparity was known

His answer on proof of disadvantage: RA 3019 requires proof not of fair and reasonable price but of manifest and gross disadvantage; the two contracts show a loss of P621,240 a month or P189,372,000 over 25 years, and Cuervo's appraisal of bare lots ignored the coming LRT stations -- 'Opinion cannot prevail over hard fact!'

His answer on jurisdiction: an error in the exercise of jurisdiction does not void a judgment, the remedy being appeal, as Faypon v. Quirino shows; the Sandiganbayan rules let the presiding justice designate two temporary justices and, by implication, revoke the designation once unanimity rendered it functus officio

His answer on the right to counsel: she was represented throughout, counsel's absences and the suspension of Atty. Coronel did not deprive her of representation, and she was finally defended by 'one of the most adroit legal minds in this country,' Atty. Estelito P. Mendoza

His Epilogue calling the lease-and-sublease a 'charade' and a 'raid against the public treasury,' and concluding that far from being denied due process she was the recipient of 'over-due' process in the Court

Justice Romero's own dissent that the lease was approved by the whole LRTA policy-making body and that a lease is a bilateral contract into which Mrs. Marcos entered as one of two indispensable parties
The book's deadline of October 10, 1998, which stopped CJP from reporting later motions or media reactions, leaving his closing appeal to the judgment of history

stances.claim: A tip from an informer, however reliable, is not personal knowledge and cannot supply probable cause for a warrantless arrest; since the police had the information the previous afternoon and could have applied for a warrant even on a Sunday, Montilla's arrest and the search that followed were invalid.
stances.rhetorical_move: line-of-precedent argument: marshalling Mengote, Burgos, Aminnudin and Encinada to show the settled requirement of personal knowledge, then exposing the majority's contradiction that the information was at once too thin for a warrant and thick enough for an arrest

stances.claim: Treating reliable tips as probable cause would place everyone at the mercy of informants and let officers manufacture urgency by timing their tips, opening loopholes for unreasonable arrests, searches and seizures.
stances.rhetorical_move: slippery-slope warning anchored in historical memory of the makapilis under Japanese occupation

stances.claim: The defense of obedience to a superior's order is obsolete: Nuremberg and the United Nations settled that the test is whether moral choice was in fact possible, and Tabuena and Peralta -- civilians, after martial law, facing no court martial -- could have defied the order or resigned.
stances.rhetorical_move: authority-plus-contrast: invoking international precedent and then showing the accused faced far less compulsion than those it condemned

stances.claim: Mrs. Marcos may be held liable under RA 3019 because the statute punishes 'entering' into a disadvantageous contract, not merely signing one, and as chair of both the LRTA and the PGHFI she knowingly contracted virtually with herself and never sought to undo the arrangement.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual parsing of the operative verb followed by inference from her double capacity and her silence after the disparity became known

stances.claim: The lease and sublease contracts are themselves the proof of manifest and gross disadvantage -- P621,240 lost monthly and P189,372,000 over 25 years -- and no expert opinion on fair rental value can overcome that documentary fact.
stances.rhetorical_move: fact-over-opinion argument, reinforced by arithmetic and by showing the appraiser valued bare lots without the coming LRT stations

stances.claim: The Sandiganbayan's irregularities, even if assumed, were errors in the exercise of jurisdiction correctable on appeal rather than defects voiding the judgment, and the presiding justice who may designate two temporary justices may also revoke the designation once unanimity renders it functus officio.
stances.rhetorical_move: jurisdiction-versus-procedure distinction supported by precedent and by the silence of the Sandiganbayan rules

stances.claim: A realistic appreciation of the physical and tactical problems of law enforcement should temper judicial scrutiny of warrantless arrests, rather than viewing police work from the placid and clinical environment of judicial chambers.
stances.rhetorical_move: the majority's position in Montilla, quoted and then rejected

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls being 'so pleased with Justice Davide's ponencia' in Malacat that he wrote a full concurrence comparing it with four warrantless-search decisions he had himself authored -- Manalili, Encinada, Lacerna and Cuison.

He describes the awkward position of dissenting from a justice he reveres: though he held and continued to hold Justice Regalado 'in great esteem,' he could not assent to the appeal for a realistic appreciation of police problems.

He recounts the detail that undid the Montilla arrest in his eyes -- the appellant was 'merely alighting from a jeepney carrying a traveling bag and a carton' when he was searched, which he asks how anyone could call being 'in the act of violating the law.'

He invokes the Nazi war criminals who justified genocide by pleading that they followed the orders of 'their adored fuehrer,' and contrasts their wartime peril with Tabuena's and Peralta's freedom to refuse or resign.

He narrates the internal mechanics that sent the Marcos case to the banc: the February 1, 1998 reorganization, Justice Francisco's retirement at 70, a Third Division reduced to four, and his own initial reservations about elevating a Motion for Reconsideration to the full Court.

He recounts Justice Kapunan's disclosure that when Chief Prosecutor Tamayo was asked at the September 10, 1998 oral argument why no independent valuation evidence was offered, he replied that if he had been the prosecutor he would have adduced it -- which CJP's colleague read as an admission of a lacking case.

He notes that the Sandiganbayan justices discussed the cases over a meal in a Quezon City restaurant, without two members of the Special Division and in the presence of a non-member -- the episode the majority turned into a due-process ground for acquittal.

He ends the chapter by explaining that his manuscript deadline of October 10, 1998 arrived days after the acquittal, leaving him to close with the reminder that what the Court wrote would still be discussed 'fifty years from now, when all of us are, in all likelihood, already in the Great Beyond.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' collects three fights in which Justice Panganiban took the side of strict legality against expedience. He begins with warrantless arrests. In Malacat v. Court of Appeals the Court, through Justice Davide, unanimously acquitted a man convicted of possessing a hand grenade, holding that a lawful arrest must precede a search and that shifty eyes and flight, without personal knowledge or an overt act, supported neither an in flagrante delicto nor a hot pursuit arrest; CJP wrote a full concurrence comparing the case with four decisions he had authored, concluding that to convict on queer behavior alone would be 'wrong, unjust and inhuman.' Six weeks later, in People v. Montilla, the majority through Justice Regalado upheld a dawn seizure of 28 kilos of marijuana made on an informer's tip and urged a realistic appreciation of police problems. Joined by Justices Melo and Puno, CJP dissented: the officers had no personal knowledge, the case paralleled Aminnudin where 'the furtive finger' of an informer triggered the arrest, and the police had held the tip since 2:00 p.m. the previous day and could have obtained a warrant even on a Sunday. He warned that accepting 'reliable tips' as probable cause would leave everyone at the mercy of informants 'reminiscent of the makapilis during the Japanese occupation,' noting with relief that the majority's pronouncement was only obiter because the issue had been waived. He next dissented in Tabuena and Peralta v. Sandiganbayan, where an 8-6 majority acquitted officials who remitted P55 million on Marcos' memorandum, calling the defense of superior orders an 'internationally discredited Nazi defense' that Nuremberg and the United Nations had already answered with the test of whether moral choice was possible, and insisting on 'justice first before mercy.' The chapter closes with his 27-page dissent from the en banc acquittal of Imelda R. Marcos in the LRTA-PGHFI lease-and-sublease cases: the statute punishes 'entering,' not signing; the two contracts prove a loss of P189 million and are 'more than enough monument to graft,' since 'Opinion cannot prevail over hard fact'; the Sandiganbayan's irregularities were errors in the exercise of jurisdiction, not defects voiding its judgment; and far from being denied due process she had received 'over-due' process. Writing against an October 10, 1998 book deadline, he ends by submitting the Court's conduct to the judgment of history.
